raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is an established non-pharmacologic strategy for stroke prevention in selected patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (AF). Its rationale rests on the observation that the left atrial appendage (LAA) is the dominant site of thrombus formation in AF, particularly in the absence of rheumatic mitral disease [1,2]. Anatomic heterogeneity—ostial size, depth, lobar complexity, and morphology—has procedural implications and may also relate to embolic risk [3]. LAAC aims to mechanically exclude the appendage from systemic circulation, thereby reducing cardioembolic events while limiting long-term exposure to oral anticoagulation.

Early clinical experience with the WATCHMAN device demonstrated technical feasibility but also highlighted procedure-related complications, particularly pericardial effusion and device embolization during the learning curve [4]. The pivotal PROTECT AF trial compared WATCHMAN implantation with warfarin and showed non-inferiority for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, despite early procedural hazards [5]. Longer follow-up suggested a reduction in hemorrhagic stroke and mortality relative to warfarin [6]. PREVAIL, designed with more stringent safety endpoints and broader operator experience, did not meet all prespecified efficacy non-inferiority criteria but showed improved procedural safety and low rates of late ischemic events [7]. Subsequent pooled analyses of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL supported LAAC as an alternative to warfarin, with fewer hemorrhagic strokes and major nonprocedural bleeding events over time [8-11].

Patients referred for LAAC in contemporary practice often differ from randomized trial populations: they are older, have higher CHA₂DS₂-VASc and HAS-BLED scores, and frequently have prior bleeding. The ASAP study provided early evidence that WATCHMAN implantation could be performed without a warfarin transition in patients considered unsuitable for warfarin, using dual antiplatelet therapy after implantation [12]. Registries and post-approval studies then confirmed high implantation success and lower complication rates in broader practice [15-18]. The NCDR LAAO Registry has been especially important in defining real-world outcomes, showing high procedural success but also emphasizing that pericardial effusion, major bleeding, and device-related thrombus remain clinically relevant [18].

Device-related thrombus (DRT) is one of the most important late complications. It occurs in a minority of patients but is associated with increased ischemic stroke or systemic embolism risk [14]. Predictors include patient factors, suboptimal device position, incomplete endothelialization, and antithrombotic regimen. Peridevice leak is also common, although small leaks were initially considered of uncertain consequence; later analyses suggest that residual communication may carry incremental thromboembolic risk, particularly when persistent or larger [13]. These observations support careful follow-up imaging—usually transesophageal echocardiography or cardiac computed tomography—and individualized antithrombotic management.

Antithrombotic therapy after LAAC remains an evolving area. Trial protocols commonly used short-term warfarin plus aspirin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy, whereas real-world practice includes direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), single antiplatelet therapy, dual antiplatelet therapy, or no therapy in extreme bleeding risk. Registry data suggest considerable variation in discharge regimens, with anticoagulant-based strategies often associated with less early adverse outcome than dual antiplatelet therapy alone, although confounding by indication is substantial [19]. Consensus documents therefore emphasize tailoring therapy to bleeding risk, DRT risk, imaging findings, and device type rather than a single universal regimen [28,30].

Comparative evidence against DOACs is particularly important because DOACs have replaced warfarin for most eligible AF patients. PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk patients to LAAC or DOAC therapy and found LAAC non-inferior for a composite of thromboembolism, cardiovascular death, major bleeding, or procedure/device-related complications [20]. Longer-term follow-up showed maintained non-inferiority and suggested less clinically relevant bleeding after the initial postprocedural period [21]. These data support LAAC mainly for patients with high thromboembolic risk and bleeding concerns, rather than as routine replacement for DOACs in low-bleeding-risk patients.

Several devices are now available. The Amplatzer Cardiac Plug and Amulet use a lobe-and-disc design, potentially advantageous for certain anatomies [24-26]. The Amulet IDE trial demonstrated non-inferiority of Amulet compared with WATCHMAN for safety and effectiveness, with higher complete occlusion but somewhat different procedural considerations [22]. The WATCHMAN FLX was designed to improve deliverability, sealing, and safety; PINNACLE FLX showed high implant success and low major complication rates [23]. Epicardial suture ligation with the LARIAT represented another percutaneous approach, but concerns about pericardial complications and variable closure durability have limited its role [27].

Imaging is central to patient selection, procedural planning, and surveillance. Transesophageal echocardiography remains widely used to exclude pre-existing thrombus, size the appendage, guide transseptal puncture and deployment, and evaluate leaks and DRT. Cardiac computed tomography provides complementary information on LAA morphology, landing-zone dimensions, and device simulation, and may be particularly useful in complex anatomy or equivocal echocardiographic assessment [29].

In summary, percutaneous LAAC has matured from a technically challenging procedure into a validated stroke-prevention option for selected AF patients, especially those with contraindications to long-term anticoagulation or unacceptable bleeding risk. The strongest evidence supports careful selection, experienced operators, meticulous imaging, and structured follow-up. Ongoing priorities include defining optimal post-implant antithrombotic therapy, clarifying the clinical significance of residual leak, improving prevention and treatment of DRT, and determining which patients benefit most compared with contemporary DOAC therapy.
